title: Audit Workspace Friction Before Buying More Gear
subtitle: Change the layout around the task, one reversible step at a time.
description: Inspect where a workspace makes the actual task harder to see, reach, switch, connect, or reset; change one layout variable; and keep the change only when it removes friction without creating a new problem.

lifeOsSource.hack: Design the workspace around the work you actually do: find one recurring reach, visibility, glare, cable, switching, or setup problem and change that variable before buying more equipment.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one frequent task, walk through it slowly, note every unnecessary reach, obstruction, visibility issue, cable move, device swap, or reset, rank the friction points, change one reversible layout variable, use the task again, and keep or undo the change based on what became easier or harder.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which step in the task had avoidable friction, what single workspace change did I make, and did it remove that friction without moving the problem somewhere else?

faq.question: Do I need to buy ergonomic equipment first?
faq.answer: No. Start by observing the task and the current layout. Moving a monitor, relocating a frequently used device, routing a cable, or clearing a reach path may solve the actual friction without a purchase.

faq.question: Is this a guide for treating pain or preventing injury?
faq.answer: No. This protocol is about workspace layout and task friction. Persistent pain, numbness, weakness, or other health concerns belong with an appropriate workplace or health professional rather than this checklist.

intro.html: A workspace can look organized and still make the real job awkward. Review it as a small system: task, person, tools, information, cables, surfaces, light, and handoffs. The useful question is not whether the setup looks ergonomic; it is where the task repeatedly becomes harder than it needs to be.

sections.title: 1. Choose one frequent task
sections.html: Pick a task you repeat: writing, reviewing a document, joining calls, comparing two screens, drawing, packing, testing hardware, or another routine. Define its start and finish so the workspace can be judged against a concrete job.

sections.title: 2. Trace the task and mark friction
sections.html: Perform the task slowly. Note unnecessary reaching, repeated window or device switching, blocked sightlines, glare, loose cables, items that must be moved twice, missing charging access, or tools that live outside the natural work area. Record what happens rather than guessing what the ideal setup should be.

sections.title: 3. Change one reversible variable
sections.html: Move one object, change one screen position, relocate one frequently used tool, reroute one cable, or create one dedicated place for an item. Prefer changes that are easy to undo so cause and effect remain visible.

sections.title: 4. Run the task again
sections.html: Repeat the same task and compare the troublesome step. Keep the change if the task is simpler and no important new problem appears. Undo or revise it when the friction merely moved elsewhere. Buy equipment only when the remaining constraint is clear enough to name.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace unsupported productivity and discomfort outcomes, pseudo-medical posture rules, rigid dimensions and timing prescriptions, and fabricated observations with a bounded workspace-friction audit.
